sections.title: CS and AI development: temporal grounding is becoming interval-native
sections.content:
Two late-July video-grounding papers attack the same representational mistake from different directions: an event is an interval, not merely two numbers called “start” and “end.”

TimePLE makes the single-span version explicit. Instead of asking a VLM to emit two endpoint tokens or coordinates, it maps every valid span into a position-duration square and has the model emit one latent <|TIMESPAN|> representation that decodes to a joint distribution over valid intervals. Nearby points in that space correspond to nearby spans, so duration and boundary dependence are built into the output geometry instead of being left for two loosely coupled regressors to discover. The paper reports 58.9 average mIoU across four benchmarks, with the largest gains on short and medium events. TimePLE

TimeLens2 handles the harder case where the evidence may occur in several disjoint pieces. Its target is a variable-cardinality set of intervals. For reinforcement learning it converts the union of predicted intervals and the union of target intervals into one-dimensional probability distributions and computes an exact temporal Wasserstein distance between them. That makes the reward dense even when spans do not overlap, avoids explicit segment matching when cardinalities differ, and treats equivalent fragmentations more sensibly than pairwise IoU matching. Its 93K-example supervision pipeline also uses independent localization, cross-agent consensus, semantic checks and boundary refinement rather than one annotation pass. The authors report that the 2B model beats size-matched baselines across seven benchmarks, while 4B and 8B variants set their reported state of the art. TimeLens2

The general systems lesson is useful beyond VTG: choose an output space whose topology already respects the constraints of the object you are predicting. If valid intervals occupy a structured manifold but the network predicts unconstrained endpoints in Euclidean space, training must relearn validity, correlation and similarity from loss signals. Both papers are preprints, so the benchmark claims remain author-reported rather than independently reproduced.

sections.title: Technical idea: exponential histograms remember recent stream history at multiple resolutions
sections.content:
Suppose a service emits one bit per request — failure or success — and you want the number of failures in the last (N) requests. Keeping all (N) bits is exact but expensive; keeping a lifetime counter is cheap but cannot forget expired events.

The exponential histogram of Datar, Gionis, Indyk and Motwani stores the recent past at progressively coarser resolution. Conceptually, it groups 1s into timestamped buckets whose sizes are powers of two. Small buckets describe the newest part of the stream precisely. As similar-size buckets accumulate, old buckets are merged, so distant history is represented by fewer, larger summaries. When the sliding-window boundary advances, completely expired buckets disappear. Only the oldest bucket that intersects the boundary is ambiguous, and the data structure bounds the error contributed by that uncertainty.

For a ((1+\epsilon))-factor estimate of the number of 1s in the last (N) positions, the original result uses (O((1/\epsilon)\log^2 N)) bits, with a matching asymptotic lower bound. The same paper extends the idea to sums of positive integers and other windowed statistics. Datar et al., SIAM Journal on Computing

The design pattern is the interesting part: resolution should decay with age when queries care about a moving suffix rather than exact history. It is the streaming analogue of a multiscale archive — exact near “now,” compressed farther back — and shows up naturally in telemetry, rate monitoring and any online system where old observations continuously fall out of scope.

sections.title: Non-CS science: preserving lean mass during tirzepatide weight loss
sections.content:
A phase-2 trial published in Nature Medicine tested whether apitegromab, an investigational antibody that selectively inhibits activation of myostatin, could change the composition of weight lost during tirzepatide treatment rather than simply changing total weight loss.

The study randomized 102 adults with overweight or obesity to tirzepatide plus apitegromab or tirzepatide plus placebo. Among participants with a week-24 DEXA scan, mean lean-mass loss was 1.6 kg with apitegromab versus 3.5 kg with placebo, a 1.9 kg difference and about 54.9% relative preservation of lean mass. Total body-weight loss remained fairly similar — 11.2 kg versus 12.5 kg — so the intervention shifted more of the lost weight toward fat rather than merely making the scale move less. Mechanistically, that is what myostatin inhibition is supposed to do: weaken a signaling pathway that restrains skeletal-muscle growth. Nature Medicine

This is interesting but still proof-of-concept. The efficacy analysis used 43 and 44 week-24 completers, most participants were women, follow-up was short, and the primary estimates were reported with 80% confidence intervals; the paper also says the P-values were descriptive without multiplicity adjustment. Most importantly, the exploratory physical-function measures did not show a notable between-group difference. Preserving DEXA-measured lean mass is therefore a biological result, not yet evidence that the combination produces better strength, mobility or long-term clinical outcomes.

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• Romania's air-policing problem has become repeatedly kinetic. Early this morning a Spanish F-18 flying a NATO air-policing mission shot down a drone after it entered Romanian airspace from Moldova about 24 km north of Galați. Romania has not formally identified the drone's origin; a NATO spokesperson said it appears Russian. It is the fourth unmanned aircraft shot down over Romania this year, after Romanian F-16s downed three Russian drones in July. Repeated engagement matters more than any single incursion: NATO's eastern flank is moving from monitoring spillover to routinely making shoot/no-shoot decisions inside alliance territory. Reuters

  • Iran is trying to turn contact with “hostile” information institutions into a licensing problem. Parliament approved a bill that would criminalize interviews and other communication with media deemed hostile, including US- or Israeli-linked outlets, with six months to two years in prison; other foreign-media interviews would require notification to the intelligence ministry. The bill also reaches information-sharing and some scientific cooperation. It still needs Guardian Council review before becoming law. The political mechanism is broader than censorship after publication: it shifts control upstream by making unauthorized relationships with foreign institutions themselves legally risky. Reuters

  • One ransom payment appears to have altered the military budget of a Sahel armed network. UN experts say an approximately $50 million ransom paid in late 2025 was largely redistributed among JNIM units and played a key role in financing the group's offensive across Mali; some money also flowed to affiliated units elsewhere. The UN report does not identify the payer. JNIM is estimated at 7,000–8,000 fighters across the Sahel, about half in Mali. The scale is the key point: kidnapping is not merely tactical revenue when a single payment can materially change a regional armed group's budget. Reuters, 14 August 2026

  • The Canada–US tariff clock is now down to three days. Washington has threatened 50% tariffs on a broad set of Canadian goods from 19 August unless disputes over cars, alcohol and dairy are resolved. The latest reported US offer would reduce some tariffs, but Canadian negotiators considered it insufficient; talks have been running daily in Washington. The institutional oddity is that several US complaints concern provincial alcohol restrictions, so Ottawa is negotiating over practices it cannot simply switch off by federal decree. Unless terms move before Wednesday, the dispute becomes a test of how much leverage a federal trade negotiation has over subnational policy. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment: free time as productive human capacity
sections.content:
“Time is the room of human development.”

— Karl Marx, Value, Price and Profit (1865), section XII. Primary text

The line appears in Marx's argument about limiting the working day. He is not only saying that overwork damages workers. He gives the demand for shorter hours a positive content: time outside the labour process is the material space in which capacities, relationships, education, politics and self-directed activity can develop.

That changes the frame of the wage struggle. A higher wage can compensate for some increased extraction, but it does not automatically compensate for the loss of disposable life-time. The conflict is therefore partly over who commands the worker's finite day, not just over the price paid per hour. It is a compact bridge between Marx's value analysis and a broader conception of emancipation that cannot be reduced to consumption.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Aristotle: democracy and oligarchy are class categories before they are headcounts

“the real thing in which democracy and oligarchy differ from each other is poverty and wealth”

— Aristotle, Politics, III.8, 1279b–1280a, H. Rackham translation. Perseus

Aristotle notices a classification problem. If “democracy” simply means rule by the many and “oligarchy” rule by the few, what do we call a city where the wealthy happen to be the majority? His answer is that number is accidental: the more basic distinction is which economic stratum rules. The rich are usually few and the poor many, so class position and headcount normally coincide, but conceptually they are different variables.

The ancient citizen body was far narrower than a modern electorate, so this is not a ready-made modern democratic theory. But analytically it is useful: constitutional form can be described by voting rules while the social basis of effective rule is described separately.

Rousseau: force has to become legitimacy to reproduce itself

“The strongest is never strong enough to be always the master, unless he transforms strength into right, and obedience into duty.”

— Jean-Jacques Rousseau, The Social Contract, I.3, G. D. H. Cole translation. Wikisource

Rousseau's distinction is between causal power and normative obligation. A weapon can make someone comply, but the fact that resistance is dangerous does not itself create a duty to obey. A durable political order therefore needs a second operation: coercive advantage must be represented and accepted as rightful authority.

Put beside Aristotle, the two fragments ask different questions about rule. Aristotle asks which social group actually governs; Rousseau asks how governing power is converted into an obligation that survives beyond the immediate application of force.

sections.title: French usage: *être au taquet*
sections.content:
Être au taquet is familiar French with two closely related meanings:

  • to be maxed out / at full capacity: Je ne peux pas prendre un autre projet cette semaine, je suis au taquet.
  • to be fully on it / in top form: Pour la soutenance, elle était au taquet.

The ambiguity is useful rather than accidental. A taquet is literally a stop or block; au taquet evokes reaching the mechanical stop. Depending on context, that can mean “I have no capacity left” or “I am operating at maximum performance.” Larousse gives both senses: à la limite de ses possibilités and au meilleur de sa forme. Larousse

So je suis au taquet aujourd'hui is not automatically “I'm exhausted.” Tone and context decide whether it means overloaded or exceptionally switched on.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: Paris once had a city-scale pneumatic message network
sections.content:
Long before electronic messaging, Paris had something surprisingly close to a physical packet network under its streets. The poste pneumatique used capsules propelled through tubes by pressure differences to move written messages between offices; the public service grew out of an 1866 telegraph-support system and operated until 1984.

At its 1933 scale, the Paris network had about 427 km of tubes, making it the largest pneumatic-post network in the world. A message could be handed over and delivered to its addressee in roughly two hours. The traffic peak came during the Second World War: the source records about 4 million objects in 1940 and 16 million in 1945. Comité pour l'histoire de la Poste

The networking analogy should not be pushed too literally, but the architecture is recognizable: local access points, routed transfers, finite-capacity links and a service designed around latency guarantees rather than bulk transport. Paris had a metropolitan low-bandwidth messaging infrastructure decades before digital networking — it just moved paper in capsules instead of bits in packets.

sections.title: Puzzle: the red-bus / blue-bus paradox
sections.content:
A commuter initially has two options:

  • Car
  • Red bus

Suppose a model predicts 50% car, 50% red bus.

Now the bus company introduces a blue bus that is identical to the red bus in every relevant respect except colour. Nothing about driving a car has changed.

One intuition says the bus market should simply split: roughly 50% car, 25% red bus, 25% blue bus. But a standard multinomial-logit model with the original car:red odds preserved and symmetry between the two buses predicts one third for each option.

What assumption in the model forces the strange one-third / one-third / one-third result, and why does adding a near-duplicate bus expose it?

Bonus: what family of discrete-choice models would you reach for if you wanted red and blue bus to behave as correlated substitutes rather than independent alternatives?

Background: independence of irrelevant alternatives and the red-bus/blue-bus example
